questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a painless ulcer on his right hand that developed from a vesicle after handling animal hides. The ulcer has a black eschar surrounded by extensive non-pitting oedema with minimal pain. Gram staining of the discharge reveals large gram-positive rods in chains. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) presents as a painless ulcer with black eschar and extensive oedema. Ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice for 60 days; penicillin can be used but ciprofloxacin is preferred due to potential resistance and as post-exposure prophylaxis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old immunocompetent male presents with a painful, crusted nodule on his cheek that has been enlarging over 3 months. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with neutrophilic microabscesses and thick-walled budding yeast with broad-based buds. KOH mount confirms the organism. Which antifungal is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: This describes North American blastomycosis (Blastomyces dermatitidis) characterised by thick-walled yeast with broad-based buds and pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia. Itraconazole 200 mg/day for 6–12 months is the drug of choice for non-CNS, non-life-threatening disease. Amphotericin B is reserved for severe/CNS disease.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her lip, followed by crusting. She gives history of recurrence at the same site every 2–3 months, often triggered by sun exposure. The most appropriate prophylactic therapy to reduce recurrence frequency is:
opts: Oral acyclovir 400 mg twice daily continuously
Oral valacyclovir 2 g as a single dose at onset
Famciclovir 1500 mg single dose at prodrome
questions.exp: For frequent recurrent herpes labialis (>6 episodes/year), continuous oral suppressive therapy with acyclovir 400 mg BD or valacyclovir 500 mg once daily is recommended. Episodic therapy shortens duration but does not reduce recurrence frequency. Topical acyclovir has minimal efficacy for recurrent disease.

questions.q: A 30-year-old sexually active male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis with a clean base and indurated edges that appeared 3 weeks after an unprotected sexual encounter. VDRL is reactive at 1:32 titre. He is allergic to penicillin. What is the best alternative treatment?
opts: Ceftriaxone 1 g IM daily for 10–14 days
questions.exp: Primary/secondary syphilis in penicillin-allergic non-pregnant patients: doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days is the WHO/CDC-recommended alternative. Ceftriaxone is an option but evidence is limited. Azithromycin is no longer recommended due to macrolide resistance in T. pallidum. Erythromycin is less reliable.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male from Bihar presents with a hypopigmented patch on his forearm with definite loss of sensation and thickened greater auricular nerve. Slit-skin smear from the patch shows a BI of 0. Histopathology shows epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytes destroying the nerve bundles. What is the Ridley-Jopling classification?
questions.exp: TT leprosy: single or few hypopigmented patches with complete loss of sensation, negative bacteriology (BI=0), and histopathology showing well-formed epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytes and giant cells destroying nerves (Fite stain negative). The greater auricular nerve thickening is characteristic. BT may show similar features but usually has more lesions and incomplete nerve damage.

questions.q: A 25-year-old patient with known tuberculoid leprosy on MDT-PB develops sudden, severe pain and tenderness over the ulnar nerve at the elbow with rapid onset of claw hand over 48 hours. The correct immediate management is:
opts: Stop dapsone and add rifampicin monotherapy
Surgical neurolysis of the ulnar nerve
questions.exp: This is Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction) presenting as acute neuritis with rapid nerve function impairment. Immediate high-dose prednisolone (40–60 mg/day, tapering over 6 months) is mandatory to prevent permanent nerve damage. MDT should be continued unchanged. Surgery is considered only for steroid-refractory cases.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with malar rash, discoid lesions, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers for 6 months. ANA is positive at 1:640, anti-dsDNA is strongly positive, and complement C3/C4 are low. Skin biopsy shows vacuolar interface dermatitis with dermal mucin deposits. The band test on perilesional normal skin is positive. What does the positive lupus band test on non-lesional skin specifically indicate?
questions.exp: The lupus band test (LBT) shows immunoglobulin/complement deposition at the dermoepidermal junction. A positive LBT on non-lesional, sun-protected skin is highly specific for SLE (systemic involvement). In DLE, the band is positive in lesional skin only. SCLE shows positive LBT in lesional skin.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with violaceous plaques on his elbows, knuckles, and eyelids (heliotrope rash), along with proximal muscle weakness and elevated CK. Nail fold capillaroscopy shows dilated capillary loops and avascular areas. Which antibody, if positive, indicates the highest risk of associated malignancy?
questions.exp: In adult dermatomyositis, anti-TIF1-γ (anti-transcriptional intermediary factor 1-gamma, formerly p155/140) is the antibody most strongly associated with malignancy-associated dermatomyositis (risk ~70%). Anti-Mi-2 is associated with classic DM with favourable prognosis. Anti-Jo-1 suggests antisynthetase syndrome. Anti-MDA5 is associated with amyopathic DM and rapidly progressive ILD.

questions.q: A 65-year-old diabetic female presents with tense bullae on normal-appearing and urticated skin of her inner thighs and abdomen for 2 months. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows linear C3 and IgG along the basement membrane zone. ELISA shows antibodies against BP180 NC16A domain. The HLA association of this condition is:
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is associated with HLA-DQB1*0301. The anti-BP180 (type XVII collagen) NC16A domain antibodies are pathogenic. HLA-DR4 is associated with rheumatoid arthritis; HLA-B27 with ankylosing spondylitis; HLA-DR3 with DH, pemphigus, and SLE.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with flaccid blisters in the mouth and on the trunk for 3 months. Nikolsky sign is positive. DIF of perilesional skin shows intercellular IgG and C3 deposits in a 'chicken-wire' pattern. ELISA is positive for anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies. What is the first-line treatment to induce remission?
opts: Rituximab 1000 mg IV two doses 2 weeks apart
questions.exp: Rituximab has been approved as first-line treatment for moderate-severe pemphigus vulgaris based on the Ritux3 trial, showing superior remission rates and fewer relapses compared to standard corticosteroids. High-dose prednisolone remains an alternative. The Ritux3 protocol uses 1000 mg IV at day 0 and day 14, with a maintenance dose at month 12.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent nodule with telangiectasia on his nose, which has been slowly enlarging over 3 years. Central ulceration developed recently. Biopsy shows islands of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artifact. The most important prognostic factor for recurrence in this tumour is:
questions.exp: In basal cell carcinoma, positive surgical margins (incomplete excision) is the single most important factor predicting local recurrence. The recurrence rate after incomplete excision exceeds 30%. Morphoeic/infiltrative and micronodular subtypes are high-risk histological patterns, but margin status outweighs subtype as a standalone predictor. Perineural invasion is also high-risk but less common.

questions.q: A 50-year-old fair-skinned man presents with a 2 cm pigmented lesion on his back. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, regression structures (white scarring), irregular dots/globules, and blue-white veil. Excision biopsy confirms melanoma with Breslow thickness 1.8 mm, no ulceration, mitotic rate 1/mm². According to AJCC 8th edition, what is the recommended surgical margin?
questions.exp: AJCC 8th edition / NCCN guidelines recommend: melanoma in situ 0.5–1 cm; ≤1 mm Breslow → 1 cm margin; 1.01–2 mm → 1–2 cm (2 cm preferred); >2 mm → 2 cm margin. This tumour at 1.8 mm Breslow requires 2 cm excision margins.

questions.q: During Mohs micrographic surgery for a 1.5 cm morphoeic BCC on the nasal ala, the surgeon maps the tumour in stages, processing the tissue as horizontal frozen sections. What percentage of surgical margin is examined with this technique compared to standard bread-loafing?
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery uses horizontal en-face frozen sections that allow nearly 100% examination of all surgical margins (compared to <1% with conventional bread-loafing). This is why Mohs has the lowest recurrence rates for high-risk BCC (recurrence rate <1% for primary BCC vs ~10% for standard excision).

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman undergoes patch testing for suspected allergic contact dermatitis. Readings at 48 and 96 hours show a 3+ reaction to nickel sulfate 5% in petrolatum. A 3+ reaction is defined as:
questions.exp: ICDRG scoring: ? (doubtful) = faint erythema only; + (weak) = erythema, infiltration, papules; ++ (strong) = erythema, infiltration, discrete vesicles; +++ (extreme) = erythema, infiltration, coalescing vesicles. A 4+ or bullous reaction is occasionally added. A 3+ corresponds to coalescing (confluent) vesicles.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman on long-term minocycline for acne for 3 years develops blue-black pigmentation in acne scars and sun-exposed skin. What is the mechanism of this pigmentation?
opts: Direct deposition of minocycline-iron chelate complexes and melanin-drug complexes
questions.exp: Minocycline-induced pigmentation (Type I–III) results from deposition of minocycline metabolite–iron chelate complexes (Type I: blue-black in acne scars; Type II: blue-grey on shins; Type III: diffuse muddy-brown in sun-exposed areas). Type III involves melanin-drug complexes rather than iron chelates. It is a distinct adverse effect requiring drug cessation.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male on isotretinoin for nodular acne for 2 months develops severe depression and suicidal ideation. The mechanism linking retinoids to neuropsychiatric effects is thought to involve:
opts: Blockade of dopamine reuptake in the prefrontal cortex
Inhibition of retinoic acid signalling in the hippocampus affecting neurogenesis
Direct hepatotoxicity causing raised ammonia and encephalopathy
Vitamin A toxicity increasing intracranial pressure
questions.exp: Isotretinoin may affect CNS retinoic acid (RA) signalling in the hippocampus, reducing neurogenesis and altering serotonin/dopamine pathways. The hippocampus is rich in RA receptors. This is distinct from raised ICP (pseudotumour cerebri) which is a separate but recognised side effect. Drug withdrawal and psychiatric referral are required.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient on methotrexate for severe psoriasis develops macrocytic anaemia and mucositis. The drug's mechanism in psoriasis and its toxicity share which common pathway?
opts: Inhibition of dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) leading to reduced thymidylate synthesis
Inhibition of calcineurin reducing T-cell activation
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits DHFR, reducing dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, impairing de novo purine and thymidylate synthesis. Rapidly dividing cells (psoriatic keratinocytes, GI epithelium, bone marrow) are most affected, explaining both efficacy and toxicity. Folinic acid (not folic acid) rescues toxicity without significantly impairing the antiproliferative effect.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with generalised hyperpigmentation, vitiligo-like patches on the dorsum of hands, premature greying, and lacy pigmentation on the mucosae. Her father had the same condition and died of liver cirrhosis at 55. Which gene is most commonly mutated?
questions.exp: Dyskeratosis congenita (DC): the X-linked form (commonest) is due to DKC1 mutations (dyskerin protein). Features include the triad of lacy reticulate pigmentation of trunk/neck, nail dystrophy, and oral leukoplakia. Systemic features include bone marrow failure and liver fibrosis. Autosomal dominant DC involves TERC/TERT mutations. WRN causes Werner syndrome (progeria).

questions.q: A 20-year-old male presents with multiple flesh-coloured filiform papules around the oral commissures and verrucous papules on the dorsum of the hands and forearms. He also has acrokeratosis verruciformis (Hopf disease) features. He is concerned about malignant transformation. Which HPV genotype is most commonly associated with epidermodysplasia verruciformis?
questions.exp: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is a rare genodermatosis (EVER1/EVER2/CIB1 mutations) with inability to control betapapillomavirus infection. HPV 5 and HPV 8 account for ~80% of malignant transformation (Bowen disease/SCC in sun-exposed areas). HPV 6/11 cause anogenital warts; HPV 16/18 cause high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with a 10-day history of honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Culture grows group A Streptococcus. The most feared complication unique to streptococcal but not staphylococcal impetigo is:
questions.exp: Post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis (PSAGN) is a recognised complication of skin infection with nephritogenic strains (M-types 2, 49, 55, 57) of Group A Streptococcus. It does not occur after staphylococcal impetigo. Antibiotics can prevent rheumatic fever from pharyngeal GAS but do NOT reliably prevent PSAGN. SSSS is caused by Staph aureus phage group II exfoliatin.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male (CD4 count 80 cells/µL) presents with multiple verrucous, exophytic lesions on the perianal area. Biopsy shows koilocytes, dyskeratosis, and high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). The pathogenesis of HSIL in this setting primarily involves:
opts: E6 protein degrading p53 and E7 protein binding retinoblastoma protein (pRb)
L1 major capsid protein activating TLR4 innate immunity
E1 helicase directly causing double-strand DNA breaks
E2 protein upregulating VEGF causing hyperproliferation
questions.exp: High-risk HPV (16, 18) E6 protein binds p53 promoting its ubiquitin-mediated degradation, abrogating apoptosis. E7 binds and inactivates pRb, releasing E2F transcription factors and driving uncontrolled cell cycle progression. Together E6/E7 oncoproteins cause genomic instability and malignant transformation. L1 is a structural protein; E1 is replication helicase; E2 normally suppresses E6/E7 transcription.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with a violaceous, atrophic plaque on his trunk with central hypopigmentation and follicular plugging. Biopsy shows vacuolar interface dermatitis, hyperkeratosis, follicular plugging, basement membrane thickening, and subepidermal mucin. DIF shows IgG and C3 at the DEJ in a granular pattern. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) shows: adherent scales with carpet-tack sign (follicular plugs), central atrophy/scarring, hyperpigmented borders, and hypopigmented centres. Histology shows vacuolar interface changes, follicular plugging, BMZ thickening, mucin deposits. DIF shows granular IgG/C3 at DEJ (positive lupus band test in lesional skin). Lichen planus shows Civatte bodies, saw-tooth rete ridges, band-like lymphocytic infiltrate.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with sclerodactyly, Raynaud phenomenon, and pitting scars on her fingertips for 2 years. Nailfold capillaroscopy shows giant capillaries and capillary loss (scleroderma pattern). Anti-centromere antibody is strongly positive. Which clinical scenario is she at highest risk for?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is the hallmark of limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc/CREST syndrome). ACA positivity is associated with a high risk of isolated pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) — occurring in up to 15% — without significant ILD. Scleroderma renal crisis is associated with dcSSc and anti-RNA polymerase III. Severe ILD is more common with anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl70) in dcSSc.

questions.q: A 42-year-old male presents with well-demarcated, silvery scaly plaques on his elbows, knees, and scalp. Histopathology of an active lesion shows parakeratosis, absence of granular layer, dilated tortuous capillaries in the dermal papillae, and Munro's microabscesses. Which cytokine is the primary driver of epidermal hyperproliferation in plaque psoriasis?
questions.exp: The IL-23/Th17 axis is central to psoriasis pathogenesis. IL-23 (from dendritic cells) drives Th17 differentiation. IL-17A causes keratinocyte hyperproliferation and antimicrobial peptide production. IL-22 (from Th22 and Th17 cells) drives acanthosis and inhibits keratinocyte differentiation (causing absence of granular layer). IL-4/IL-13 are key in atopic dermatitis; IL-31 mediates itch; IFN-γ plays a role but is not the primary driver.

questions.q: A 6-month-old infant presents with intensely pruritic erythematous papules and vesicles on the cheeks, scalp, and extensor surfaces of limbs since 2 months of age. Total serum IgE is markedly elevated. The barrier defect in this condition is most commonly caused by mutations in:
questions.exp: Atopic dermatitis (AD) has a strong association with loss-of-function mutations in FLG (filaggrin gene), present in 30–50% of moderate-severe AD cases in European populations. Filaggrin is essential for stratum corneum barrier function; its deficiency causes transepidermal water loss and allergen sensitisation. SPINK5 mutations cause Netherton syndrome; ABCA12 mutations cause lamellar ichthyosis/harlequin ichthyosis; COL7A1 causes dystrophic EB.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with irregular depigmented patches on her face and hands for 1 year. Wood's lamp shows chalk-white fluorescence (brilliant white). Dermoscopy shows perilesional hyperpigmentation (perifollicular and marginal repigmentation). She is started on narrowband UVB. The target cells destroyed in this condition are:
questions.exp: Vitiligo results from selective autoimmune destruction of melanocytes (melanocyte-specific CD8+ cytotoxic T cells). The autoantigen includes Melan-A/MART-1 and tyrosinase-related proteins. Wood's lamp accentuates the depigmentation (chalk-white due to complete melanocyte loss). Perilesional perifollicular hyperpigmentation on dermoscopy indicates presence of residual follicular melanocyte reservoir, predicting better response to treatment.

questions.q: A 20-year-old female presents with acquired hypermelanosis on bilateral cheekbones and forehead for 3 years, worsening with sunlight and during pregnancy. Dermoscopy shows a predominantly epidermal pattern (accentuation under Wood's lamp). First-line topical treatment combining depigmenting, anti-inflammatory, and sunscreen properties is:
questions.exp: Kligman's modified triple combination formula (hydroquinone 4–5% + tretinoin 0.05–0.1% + low-potency corticosteroid) remains the gold standard for melasma. It addresses multiple pathways: HQ inhibits tyrosinase; tretinoin increases keratinocyte turnover; corticosteroid reduces inflammation and mitigates irritancy. Tri-Luma cream (HQ 4% + tretinoin 0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) is the commercial preparation.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with diffuse hair shedding on the vertex and frontotemporal scalp for 2 years with a positive pull test. Trichoscopy shows peripilar signs (brown halos), vellus hairs, and single-hair follicular units replacing terminal hair units. Serum DHT levels are elevated. The target enzyme inhibited by finasteride is:
questions.exp: Androgenetic alopecia (male pattern) is predominantly mediated by DHT acting on androgen receptors in hair follicles. Finasteride (1 mg/day) selectively inhibits 5α-reductase type 2 (predominant isoform in scalp), reducing DHT production. Dutasteride inhibits both type 1 and type 2. Aromatase inhibition would increase androgens. 5α-reductase type 1 is the target in prostate cancer; its inhibition by finasteride is less relevant for AGA.

questions.q: A 28-year-old female presents with nail changes: pitting, onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, and oil-drop sign on multiple fingernails. She also has scaly plaques on the scalp. Which nail change is most specific for psoriatic arthritis involvement?
questions.exp: While pitting occurs in both nail psoriasis and alopecia areata, in the context of psoriasis, nail pitting (especially geometric/regular pitting) is most closely associated with psoriatic arthritis — present in >80% of PsA patients. In fact, nail psoriasis (particularly pitting + onycholysis) is one of the strongest predictors of progression to PsA. Leukonychia, erythronychia, and Beau's lines are non-specific systemic/local findings.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a non-healing ulcer on his lower leg for 8 months. The ulcer has a punched-out appearance with undermined edges, and satellite lesions. Biopsy shows tuberculoid granulomas with caseous necrosis. PCR for Mycobacterium is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis and the treatment of choice?
opts: Lupus vulgaris — anti-TB therapy for 9 months
Buruli ulcer (Mycobacterium ulcerans) — rifampicin + streptomycin for 8 weeks
Tuberculosis cutis orificialis — anti-TB therapy for 6 months
questions.exp: Buruli ulcer caused by M. ulcerans presents as a painless undermined ulcer with satellite lesions on the lower extremities. The mycobacterium produces mycolactone toxin causing necrosis and immunosuppression. Standard WHO treatment is rifampicin 10 mg/kg/day + streptomycin 15 mg/kg/day for 8 weeks. Lupus vulgaris is a more nodular, soft lesion (apple jelly sign); scrofuloderma arises from underlying lymph node TB.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunosuppressed organ transplant recipient presents with rapidly growing, keratotic nodules on his hands and forearms over 6 months. Biopsy shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, horn cysts, and papillomatosis without atypia. The condition is termed 'Stucco keratosis' in common patients, but this aggressive presentation after transplant is called:
questions.exp: Florid cutaneous papillomatosis (FCP) is a paraneoplastic syndrome and also occurs in immunosuppressed transplant recipients. In transplant patients, rapidly proliferating HPV-driven warts (verrucae vulgares) presenting as hundreds of keratotic nodules is termed florid cutaneous papillomatosis (or occasionally 'verrucae in an immunosuppressed host'). In the paraneoplastic context it is associated with GI malignancies. Arsenical keratosis occurs on palms/soles; trichilemmal tumour is a scalp cystic tumour.
